hook: The peasant girl who led the French army at 17 and was burned at 19.

pages.x: Joan was born around 1412 in Domrémy, a village in north-eastern France, to a farming family. France was losing the Hundred Years' War: the English and their allies held Paris and the north, and the heir to the throne, Charles, had not even been crowned.

At 13 she began to hear voices she said were saints, telling her to drive out the English and see Charles crowned at Reims. At 16 she walked to the nearest fortress and demanded an escort to the prince. The captain laughed, then gave in.

At Chinon in 1429 Charles hid among his courtiers, dressed like them, to test her. Joan walked straight up to him. Churchmen questioned her for three weeks, then let her ride to war in armour, with her own white banner.

The English had besieged Orléans for months. Joan arrived in April 1429, and in nine days the French stormed the English forts. She was hit in the shoulder by an arrow, pulled it out, and went back into the fight. The siege was lifted.
In July 1429 she led Charles through enemy country to Reims, where he was crowned Charles VII. Joan stood by the altar holding her banner.

In 1430 she was captured at Compiègne and sold to the English. A church court at Rouen tried her for heresy, and for wearing men's clothes. On 30 May 1431, aged 19, she was burned at the stake in the market square.
Twenty-five years later a new trial declared her innocent, and in 1920 she was made a saint. Joan turned the tide of the Hundred Years' War and became the national heroine of France.
pts: Lifted the siege of Orléans at 17
Saw Charles VII crowned at Reims
A saint, and the heroine of France
